fields.blurb: The third interstellar object ever found, caught twice in one night. It moved 42 pixels in 94 minutes.
fields.lambdaLine: Wavelengths matched to within 2 percent, near 4.5 to 4.6 microns
fields.snrMethod: Aperture photometry (r = 5 px aperture, annulus 6-9 px)
story: Comet 3I/ATLAS is the third interstellar object ever found, discovered on 2025-07-01 by the ATLAS survey in Chile. It crossed perihelion on 2025-10-29 at about 1.36 au from the Sun. On 2025-12-14, SPHEREx caught it twice in one night, 94 minutes apart, at about 1.806 au from Earth.

In 94 minutes the comet moved 42.27 pixels against the star field, about 167 arcseconds per hour. The blink flips between the two frames so the motion jumps out, the way a blink comparator makes a moving point of light stand out.

The predicted position lands within about 2 pixels of the measured centroid in both frames, while the comet itself jumps 42 pixels. This field is star-poor, so no star-registration number is claimed for it.
fields.title: 3I/ATLAS: One Night in December

fields.baseline: One observation by two detectors, plus the same field re-imaged 6 days later
fields.blurb: The freshest data SPHEREx has published. A mechanics field: it proves the app runs end to end on the newest release. No mover is claimed here.
fields.lambdaLine: No wavelength-matched pair in this field. The Jul 26 frame's wavelength at field center differs from the Jul 20 D1 frame by 5.3 percent, over the 2 percent limit.
fields.shiftNote: Not a blink pair. Frames a and b are two detectors over different sky from one observation, and frame c differs from frame a by 5.3 percent in wavelength at field center, over the 2 percent limit.
story: The freshest data SPHEREx has published: Quick Release 3 frames from 2026-07-20, less than four months old at demo time. One observation seen by two detectors at once, two different spectral slices of neighbouring sky, plus the same field re-imaged six days later.

This field's job is to prove the app runs on the survey's newest data end to end: load, display, wavelength readout. It is not a blink pair and no mover is claimed for it. A SkyBoT check lists only main-belt asteroids of magnitude 19.3 or fainter inside the field at both epochs, below single-frame visibility.
The auto-blink is off in this field on purpose. Use the frame chips to step through the three frames by hand.
fields.title: The Survey's Newest Data

fields.blurb: The same comet, 135 days apart. In August it was not detectable in a single frame. By December it was the brightest thing in its cutout.
fields.lambdaLine: Wavelengths matched to 0.08 percent, near 4.74 microns in both frames, the tightest match on the slate
fields.shiftNote: Tracked pair: the comet is centered in both cutouts. Between the epochs it crossed about 86 degrees of sky, so the two star fields are completely different. There is no single-frame shift to measure.
fields.snrMethod: Aperture photometry (r = 5 px aperture, annulus 6-9 px)
story: The same comet, 135 days apart. In August 2025, inbound at 2.807 au, SPHEREx's campaign frames show the star field without a detectable comet. Measured aperture signal-to-noise at the predicted pixel: 0.95. That is a non-detection, stated as a measured result, not a gap in the data. Across cleaning regimes the August number runs 0.95 to 1.14.
By December 14, post-perihelion at 1.806 au, the comet is the brightest thing in its cutout: signal-to-noise 19.5 by the same aperture method. The blink shows a source switching on.
This is a tracked then-and-now pair, not a star-field blink. The August epoch is labeled below single-frame detection (SNR about 1) so the demo never claims a visible August comet.
fields.title: 3I/ATLAS: The Awakening

fields.blurb: The fourth-largest asteroid in the main belt, caught twice in 21 hours. It jumped 68 pixels.
fields.lambdaLine: Wavelengths matched to within 1 percent, 4.43 to 4.46 microns
fields.snrMethod: Unmasked aperture photometry at the measured centroid (r = 5 px)
story: Hygiea is the fourth-largest asteroid in the main belt. In late September 2025, two months before its December opposition window, SPHEREx caught it twice, 21 hours apart, at about magnitude 11.3. In 21 hours it moved 68.01 pixels against the star field, about 20 arcseconds per hour.
The predicted position lands within about 0.35 pixels of the measured centroid in both frames, while the object itself jumps 68 pixels.

The two epochs' aperture fluxes must not be read as a brightness change. The flux is dominated by the flag masking, so it is a detection statistic, never a brightness claim. No brightness-change claim is made for Hygiea.
fields.title: Hygiea: The Giant, in 21 Hours

fields.blurb: The largest object in the asteroid belt, bright enough to saturate the detector. It jumped 67 pixels in a single day.
fields.lambdaLine: Wavelengths matched to within 1 percent, 4.44 to 4.48 microns
fields.snrMethod: Unmasked aperture photometry at the measured centroid (r = 5 px)
story: Ceres is a dwarf planet and the largest object in the asteroid belt. On 2025-07-10 the survey caught it twice in a single day, 16 hours apart. It is so bright its core pixels carry saturation-class flags: zeroing flagged pixels would cut its aperture flux about a hundredfold, so these cutouts were cleaned with zodiacal-light subtraction only and no flag masking.
In 16 hours it moved 67.39 pixels. The predicted position lands within about 0.3 pixels of the measured centroid in both frames.
Signal-to-noise by unmasked aperture photometry: 419.6 and 403.5. The strongest photometry on the slate, and the core clips white by design.
fields.title: Ceres: The Largest Asteroid
